title: Memories of a Pump Jockey
summary: When I was a teenager, one rite of passage was to have a job at a gas station. Modern life has dispensed with their dispensers, and everyone outside of New Jersey pumps their own gas now, but from 1972 to 1982, I was a pump jockey. I started at a small, independent Union 76 station […]
body_markdown:
When I was a teenager, one rite of passage was to have a job at a[gas station](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/when-service-stations-had-outsize-influence-on-small-town-america/) . Modern life has dispensed with their dispensers, and everyone outside of New Jersey pumps their own gas now, but from 1972 to 1982, I was a pump jockey.


I started at a small, independent Union 76 station in the California desert town of Mojave, where I pumped gas and swabbed the deck. The heat and the hard concrete were reminders of what would happen if you didn’t eat your Wheaties and do your homework. My feet always hurt. My hands and face were always covered with grease, and I was always uncomfortable in some way, but working with the public was usually fun and exciting. Fixing cars and tires, however, was not, and I had many misadventures because I was clumsy and unmechanical. All these years later, I still feel bad for customers who ended up having me fix anything, even though my intentions were always good.


Hum Images/Universal Images Group via Getty Images


It was a minimum-wage job, of course—$1.65 per hour back then, so if you worked 20 hours a week, you got $33. Sometimes, you would sell a filler or additive, and there was a plastic ring in the bottom you could turn in for 50 cents. We all thought that was a great bonus. I lived at home and was just glad to have any kind of spending money for my own gas or whatever else came up. Before the energy crisis, gas was[39 cents per gallon](https://www.hagerty.com/media/hagerty-community/according-to-you-service-station-stories/) , so you didn’t need that much money to get around anyway.


One station I worked at, however, paid by the gallon—3 cents per—rather than hourly. So I kept a 3×5 card in my back pocket on which I wrote the total of each fill: 8 gallons, 20 gallons, what have you. This was an accounting nightmare, of course, but the owner thought we would be more careful to fill up every tank and make a few extra pennies on each fill. We were encouraged to fill tanks to the brim. The recommendation now is not to do that, and to stop when the pump cuts off, but to the owners in that day, every drop counted, and filling the tank after the pump stopped was crucial. As was selling every potential quart of oil and filter.


When a car pulled up, one or more pump jockeys would go to the car, wash the windows, fill ’er up, check the tires, and open the hood to see what was going on under there. Check the oil, check the air filter, and check all the other accessible items, like power steering, transmission, antifreeze, and brake fluid. Then try to sell them on something.


Getty Images


We had just left the era where desert travelers carried giant canvas bags of water on the hood or the trunk (not to mention cans of gas and a couple spare tires) to provide cold refreshment—or to fill the radiator in a pinch—and most cars did well in the Mojave with their factory antifreeze containers.


Over the years, I worked at both small-town gas stations, giant stations on the Grapevine, and company stations.


As I said, working on cars wasn’t my forte. Any part you took off went into the solvent, which was simply a machine that sat on a barrel of solvent and pumped it up to clean, then recirculated it so nothing was lost. I must have been a magnet for static electricity, though, because I was always shocking myself every time I touched it. I learned to stay away from that machine.


I did, however, learn to measure the fuel tanks in the ground, so I could do the math on how much was needed when the 8800-gallon tank wagons arrived. These were the semitrucks that kept us stocked. You had to measure the tanks with a stick, and I would have the truck driver do it, too, because if there was a mistake and insufficient room in the tank, then he couldn’t offload the gas.


Getty Images


At the small operations, we were usually at the bottom of our tanks. No small operator wanted his tanks completely full; he wanted to never run out while also having minimum money in inventory. **** It was a balancing act. Company stations were the opposite: They wanted their tanks filled as soon as there was room in them. So I had to learn to game out the scenarios and daily gas usage—which was different every day—using back-of-envelope calculations to make sure tanks never ran out for small operators and to make sure tanks were always full for company operations.


For the small guys, when the tank wagon came, you had to hand them the money before they dropped the gas. This was a pile of credit card slips, along with a check from the boss for the difference. Part of my job was adding up all those $1 and $2 and $3 slips, banding them together with totals, and then getting a check for the balance every time there was a gas delivery. Big company stations, on the other hand, just kept an account, and you didn’t have to deal with paying the truck driver.


Hum Images/Universal Images Group via Getty Images


I have fond memories of those times, the cars I saw and the people I encountered. The Cadillacs with their giant hoods—I could barely get them up all the way, and then once I had, how easy it seemed to get lost beneath them. The exciting Jaguars with their dual gas tanks, one on each side. So many cars with the filler behind the rear license plate, and I had to squat down to get at it. Big-shot doctors with dictating equipment beside them, and cowboys in their trucks.


We didn’t sell food or drinks; we sold fuel and oil and parts. Air was free, water was free, and so was our labor with your fill-up. Such a long time ago in a very different place.
